node.text: What is the message text replacement rule?

A message text replacement rule generally refers to an automated condition or pattern configured to swap, expand, sanitize, or reformat text within messages before they are sent, logged, displayed, or routed. ​Because the term appears across several domains, its exact implementation depends on the system in which it is used: ​1. Operating Systems & Messaging (Text Shortcuts / Snippets) ​In mobile and desktop operating systems (e.g., iOS, macOS, Android, Windows) and productivity tools (e.g., TextExpander): ​What it is: A user-defined mapping between a short abbreviation (trigger phrase) and a longer snippet of text. ​Rule structure: ​Shortcut \rightarrow Phrase (e.g., typing omw automatically expands to On my way!). ​Behavior: When the trigger pattern is typed and followed by a delimiter (like a space or punctuation), the system replaces the shortcut string with the defined target phrase. ​2. SMS Gateways & Network Message Routing (e.g., Ozeki, SMPP Proxies) ​In telecommunications, SMS routers, and notification gateways, message replacement rules intercept SMS/chat traffic in-flight: ​What it is: A filter applied during message routing that modifies the content or metadata of a message dynamically. ​Common syntax: Often implemented via regular expressions (e.g., sed/Perl syntax s/<pattern>/<replacement>/). ​Typical use cases: ​Appending disclaimers or ads: Matching the entire body s/^(.*)$/$1 Reply STOP to opt out/. ​Character translation/normalization: Converting non-GSM characters into plain ASCII equivalents to prevent multi-segment billing. ​Number/Recipient remapping: Rewriting prefixes or recipient numbers on outbound routes. ​3. Log Management, Monitoring, & SIEM (e.g., Syslog, Splunk, Logstash) ​In event monitoring and centralized logging: ​What it is: A parsing rule that searches for specific strings or regex patterns within incoming log message payloads and transforms them. ​Typical use cases: ​Data masking / Redaction: Replacing sensitive data (PII, passwords, credit card numbers, auth tokens) with placeholders like [REDACTED] or hashes before storing. ​Normalization: Replacing variable system paths, hostnames, or timestamps with standardized tokens to enable consistent grouping and aggregation. ​4. Chatbots, Relay Bots, & Social Platforms (e.g., Telegram / Discord Forwarders) ​In feed relays and community bots: ​What it is: A pre-forwarding or post-processing rule that edits the original post before republishing it to another channel. ​Typical use cases: ​Stripping source links, invite URLs, or user mentions (@username). ​Replacing source affiliate tags with custom referral codes. ​Translating specific keywords or inserting custom footers. ​If you are working with a specific platform, framework, or standard (such as an SMS gateway, syslog daemon, operating system shortcut, or a particular software API), share the platform name for the exact syntax and configuration steps.
